`var` shares one binding across iterations; you want a fresh binding per iteration.
The IIFE pattern is the manual version of the same fix, worth recognizing in legacy code.

exercises.prompt:
Implement `memoize(fn)` — return a function that caches results keyed by arguments, so repeated calls with the same arguments invoke `fn` only once.

Example calls and expected output:

```js
let calls = 0;
const add = memoize((a, b) => { calls += 1; return a + b; });
console.log(add(2, 3));  // 5
console.log(add(2, 3));  // 5 (cached, fn not re-run)
console.log(add(4, 5));  // 9
console.log(calls);      // 2
```

```
5
5
9
2
```

Forward arguments with rest/spread so the wrapped function receives them.
exercises.prompt:
Implement `once(fn)` — return a function that invokes `fn` at most one time and returns the cached result on every later call. The standard shape for lazy singletons and init guards.

Example calls and expected output:

```js
let n = 0;
const init = once(() => { n += 1; return n; });
console.log(init());  // 1
console.log(init());  // 1 (fn not re-run)
console.log(n);       // 1
```

```
1
1
1
```

exercises.prompt:
Implement `createCounter(start)` returning `{ inc, dec, get, reset }`. The count must be **truly private** — no property on the returned object may expose it (`c.count` must be `undefined`).

c.inc();

undefined

lessons.comparisonNote: `let` behaves like Java locals — block-scoped, must be declared before use — so make it your default mental model. `var`'s function scope and hoist-to-`undefined` have no Java analog; treat `var` as legacy syntax you'll read but never write. The TDZ is JS enforcing at runtime what Java enforces at compile time: no use before declaration.
keyPoints: Scope is lexical: bindings resolve where code is written, not where it runs.
`var` is function-scoped and hoisted to `undefined`; `let`/`const` are block-scoped with a TDZ.
Reading a `let`/`const` before its declaration throws `ReferenceError` — that's the TDZ.
`const` freezes the binding, not the value: object contents stay mutable.
`for (let i...)` rebinds `i` fresh each iteration — the mechanism behind the loop fix.
lessons.title: Lexical Scope, var/let/const & the TDZ

lessons.comparisonNote: Java lambdas capture *effectively final* variables — essentially a copy of the value at capture time. JavaScript closures capture the variable itself, live. That single difference is why the loop bug is impossible in Java and classic in JS: Java's loop variable couldn't be captured non-finally at all, while JS hands every iteration's callback the same mutable binding.
keyPoints: A closure captures live variable bindings, not value snapshots — later mutations are visible inside.
The loop-var bug: `var` shares one binding across iterations, so deferred callbacks all see the final value.
`let` fixes it with per-iteration bindings; the IIFE fix does the same thing manually.
Multiple closures over one scope share its state — the mechanism behind private-state patterns.
Tracing "what will this log" means tracing which *binding* each function closed over.
lessons.title: Closure Mechanics & the Loop-Var Bug

lessons.comparisonNote: Java does memoization with an explicit `ConcurrentHashMap` field and privacy with `private` fields — both require a class and ceremony. In JS the factory function *is* the class: closed-over locals are instance fields that no reflection can reach. When you need per-instance private state in a hurry, reach for a closure before reaching for a class.
keyPoints: `memoize` trades memory for time — the cache lives in the closure, invisible and tamper-proof.
`once` is the zero-argument specialization: lazy singletons and init guards.
The module pattern gives *true* private state — unreachable, not merely conventionally hidden.
Partial application builds specialized functions from general ones; config-first APIs are the canonical use.
Every closure keeps its environment alive — that's the feature, and (next lesson) the cost.
lessons.title: Closures as a Design Tool

lessons.comparisonNote: Same GC theory as Java: an object is collectible when unreachable. The difference is visibility — in Java you'd *see* the field holding the reference, but a JS closure's reference lives in its hidden `[[Environment]]`. So when Java instincts say "nothing references this anymore," check the closures: a registered listener or an old effect may be a GC root you can't see in the source.
keyPoints: Stale closures are the #1 React hooks bug: long-lived callbacks capture old render state.
A closure keeps its lexical environment reachable — capture the smallest value you need.
Unbounded `memoize` caches and unremoved listeners are memory leaks with respectable names.
Fix staleness with dependency arrays, functional updaters, or refs holding latest values.
Diff two heap snapshots to find retained closures; check listeners and caches first.
lessons.title: Stale Closures & Memory Retention
